    "student_name": "Alex Johnson",
    "title": "Real-World Economic Case Study: Analyzing Price Changes, Consumer Behavior, and Quantitative Outcomes",
    "learning_objectives": [
      "Apply economic theories such as supply and demand, price elasticity, and consumer choice to a real-world scenario.",
      "Enhance quantitative analysis skills by calculating price changes, elasticity, and simple regression-based estimates.",
      "Use visual aids such as graphs, tables, and interactive data tools to interpret economic patterns.",
      "Connect economic concepts to practical decision-making in businesses, households, or public policy."
    ],
    "task_description": "Alex will investigate a local business or consumer market, such as coffee shops, grocery stores, ride-sharing services, or movie tickets, to analyze how price changes affect customer demand and business revenue.     "activity_steps": [
      "Choose one real-world market, such as a local coffee shop, convenience store, or streaming service.",
      "Identify a price change that has occurred, such as an increase in the price of coffee, a discount on snacks, or a change in subscription fees.",
      "Collect or use a dataset showing price, quantity demanded, and total revenue before and after the price change.",
      "Create a table summarizing the data.",
      "Calculate the percentage change in price and the percentage change in quantity demanded.",
      "Calculate price elasticity of demand using the formula: elasticity = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price.",
      "Interpret whether demand is elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic based on the elasticity value.",
      "Create a supply and demand graph or price-quantity graph to visualize the change.",
      "Explain how the price change affects total revenue using the elasticity result.",
      "Discuss one practical business or policy implication of the findings, such as whether the firm should increase, decrease, or maintain the price."
    ],
    "visual_and_interactive_components": [
      "Use a spreadsheet or graphing tool to create a line graph showing price and quantity over time.",

      "sample_formula_examples": [
        "Percentage change in price = (new price - old price) / old price × 100",
        "Percentage change in quantity demanded = (new quantity - old quantity) / old quantity × 100",
        "Price elasticity of demand = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price",
        "Total revenue = price × quantity demanded"
      ]
    },
    "case_study_prompt": "Imagine you are an economic consultant for a local coffee shop. The owner is considering increasing the price of a medium coffee from $3.50 to $4.25. Data shows that before the increase, the shop sold 400 medium coffees per week, and after the increase, it sold 340 per week. Analyze whether this price increase is likely to increase or decrease total revenue, and recommend a pricing strategy based on your findings.",
    "deliverables": [
      "A short written analysis explaining the economic theory applied.",
      "A completed data table with before-and-after price, quantity, and revenue values.",
      "One or two visual graphs showing the price change and demand response.",
      "Elasticity calculation with interpretation.",
      "A final recommendation to the business based on the quantitative results."

      "Spreadsheet software such as Excel, Google Sheets, or a simple graphing calculator.",

  "options": [
    "A. The proposer may choose an arbitrary new value as long as n is larger than every proposal number seen in the PREPARE responses.",
    "B. The proposer must receive responses from a majority quorum, and if any response indicates a previously accepted proposal, it must propose the value associated with the highest-numbered accepted proposal seen; if none is indicated, it may propose an arbitrary value.",
    "C. The proposer must wait until every acceptor responds to PREPARE(n) before it can decide, because a non-responding acceptor might have accepted a higher-numbered proposal.",
    "D. The proposer can ignore previously accepted values if its own proposal number n is strictly greater than all accepted proposal numbers reported by the quorum."
  ],
  "correct_answer": "B",
  "explanation": "Paxos safety depends on quorum intersection and the invariant that once a value is accepted, no higher-numbered proposal may choose a different value. A proposer must hear from a majority quorum; if any member of that quorum has accepted a proposal, the proposer must adopt the value with the highest proposal number among those accepted values. It only has freedom to choose an arbitrary value when no accepted value was reported by the responding quorum. It does not need responses from all acceptors, and it cannot override an already accepted value merely because its own proposal number is larger."
}
